title: Sappho's ‘Brother Poem’ caused a sensation, but may have come from looted antiquities
dek: The Sappho ‘Brother Poem’ papyrus published in 2014 had holders provide three or four contradictory accounts of its discovery; Egypt was in political upheaval at the time, and scholars widely suspect it emerged via black-market looting, with authenticity unconfirmed to this day.
why: Almost all of Sappho's surviving poetry consists of fragments; this episode explains how they were pieced together from garbage heaps and mummy cartonnage, and why a ‘newly discovered’ poem remains unaccepted by mainstream scholarship.
who: Readers interested in classical philology, artifact authentication, and ancient Greek ideas about gender and desire—especially those wanting to understand how scholars handle artifacts of uncertain provenance.

points.h: Sappho's biography is almost entirely reconstructed from her own poems
points.body: Sappho was a poet of ancient Greece's Archaic period (c. 620–570 BCE), from the island of Lesbos, only 36 kilometers from Turkey. Biographical sources about her are sparse; the most reliable details come from her own poems: she had a daughter, Cleis, mentioned brothers, but never a husband. She came from a wealthy family and received elite education in Homer and choral performance, later going into exile in Sicily with her family due to factional political conflict. The term ‘Lesbian’ does derive from her reputation, but the word itself wasn't coined to describe her until the mid-18th century—applying it to Sappho herself is anachronistic.

points.h: Only 650 lines survive from Sappho's approximately 10,000 poems
points.body: Sappho is said to have composed about 10,000 lines of poetry, which the ancient Library of Alexandria organized into nine books, but most of it is lost. Only about 650 lines survive: two complete poems—the Hymn to Aphrodite (Poem 1) and Poem 58 on old age (discovered only in the early 21st century)—plus nearly complete Poems 16 and 31, and roughly 200 fragments, some just single words. Her work didn't disappear due to systematic destruction (like the often-cited myth of ‘Christian book-burning’, which is explicitly refuted), but rather due to the simple precarity of how ancient texts survived.

points.h: Most surviving Sappho fragments come from an ancient Egyptian garbage dump
points.body: The primary source of surviving Sappho poetry is the Oxyrhynchus papyri, which came from an ancient garbage dump in Egypt where massive quantities of casually discarded papyrus fragments were excavated in the 19th and 20th centuries—invoices, tax returns, private letters—interspersed with references to ancient authors, including Sappho. Other fragments are preserved in ancient texts like Longinus's On the Sublime; the famous Poem 31 fragment was rediscovered in an 1554 manuscript copy of Longinus's work, a discovery that directly sparked a Sappho craze during the Renaissance.

points.h: The sensational Brother Poem's claimed provenance does not withstand scrutiny
points.body: In 2004, the Cologne papyrus—actually mummy-wrapping cartonnage—yielded a complete text of Poem 58, the ‘old-age poem’, with clear provenance and no scholarly dispute. But the ‘Brother Poem’ announced in 2014 is entirely different: its holder gave three or four contradictory accounts of its discovery and never confirmed the source. Egypt was in violent political upheaval at the time, making looting and black-market circulation highly likely. Some Sappho scholars have included the Brother Poem in new translations, but Marguerite Johnson's own position is clear: she confidently cites the old-age poem but deliberately avoids using the Brother Poem for now.

points.h: Sappho invented the concept of ‘bittersweet’ love
points.body: When we speak of love as ‘bittersweet’, the concept comes directly from Sappho's Fragment 130: a Greek compound word joining 'sweet' (glukus) and 'bitter' (pikros). In her work, Eros—closer to desire than love—is not a god to be appeased but an unconquerable beast that loosens one's limbs and destroys reason in an instant. This echoes the Homeric logic where heroes' emotional loss of control brings disaster: like her male contemporaries, Sappho views this uncontrolled force with deep wariness.

points.h: Poem 1 depicts power imbalance, not a female utopia
points.body: Some readers interpret Sappho as depicting a utopia of equal love between women, but Marguerite Johnson disagrees. In Poem 1, the Hymn to Aphrodite, the goddess explicitly says she will ‘violate that woman's will’, thereby making her love Sappho—the same power structure as later Greek pederasty, just between women. The poem may even bear traces of curse-tablet magic: such spells often featured crude language about dragging someone by the hair, a brutal coercion formula.

points.h: Sappho expressed relativism about beauty a generation before Protagoras
points.body: In Fragment 16, Sappho says that while others consider cavalry, infantry, or fleets the most beautiful things on earth, she believes beauty is whatever one desires—a relativism almost identical to Protagoras's later claim that ‘man is the measure of all things’, yet Sappho may have expressed it a generation earlier. She supports this through Helen's story: Helen abandoned her husband and children for Paris because she followed her own desire, not the male value system of war and honor celebrated in Homer's epics.

points.h: Each era reshapes Sappho in its own image
points.body: From 19th-century suffragists using her as a symbol of a ‘forgotten female genius’ to second-wave feminists in the 1970s reading her as an openly queer pioneer, Sappho has been repeatedly appropriated and projected by different eras. Marguerite Johnson's stance is clear: readers can reimagine Sappho freely, but scholars must keep that imaginative projection separate from textual analysis—the two must never mix.
